talks.title: 2022 - Life and death of an iOS attacker by Luca Todesco
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding 2022 - Life and death of an iOS attacker by Luca Todesco.
talks.summary:
Overview: Luca Todesco presents at Hexacon on the life and death of an iOS attacker, surveying Apple's aggressive security hardening and its impact on jailbreak and exploit development.

Key Topics: Pointer authentication codes (PAC) on A12+ devices; iOS CFI properties preventing pointer substitution; Apple's rapid security improvements; the shrinking window for public jailbreaks; and ideas for future research directions.

Technical Details: Todesco explains PAC tagging pointers with unpredictable signatures to block traditional exploitation, and how compile-time CFI instrumentation protects function pointers and return addresses. He discusses techniques that died and potential new approaches.

Takeaways: Apple's security investment has dramatically raised exploitation costs. Researchers must adapt to PAC, CFI, and other mitigations while identifying remaining attack surfaces.

talks.title: 2022 - The unavoidable pain of backups by Nicolas Devillers, Anaïs Gantet & Mouad Abouhali
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of 2022 - The unavoidable pain of backups by Nicolas Devillers, Anaïs Gantet & Mouad Abouhali.
talks.summary:
Why Target Backup Software

Airbus Security Lab researchers evaluate NetBackup because backups are resilience-critical, widely deployed (claimed 87% of Fortune Global 500), highly privileged, and move sensitive data at scale. Prior work includes Immunity’s remote execution and Google’s remote code execution disclosures.

NetBackup Domain Architecture

A domain includes clients on backed-up systems, a primary server orchestrating policies and catalogs, media servers storing to disk or tape libraries, and OpsCenter for monitoring. Trust flows from OpsCenter to primaries and from primaries to clients and media servers.

Research Methodology

The team guided analysis with security questions: attackers need internal knowledge and tooling; a NetBackup client can compromise higher-privilege components; clients may pivot laterally; and attackers may target metadata needed for restore. They iterated documentation review, operator interviews, lab setup, and binary analysis—planning to present four findings and an end-to-end attack scenario, though detailed vulnerabilities extend beyond introductory architecture coverage in the available recording.

talks.title: 2022 - You've got mail! And I'm root on your Zimbra server by Thomas Chauchefoin
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of 2022 - You've got mail! And I'm root on your Zimbra server by Thomas Chauchefoin.
talks.summary:
Why Zimbra Is a High-Value Target

Thomas Chauchefoin of Sonar describes Zimbra as a widely deployed all-in-one mail platform used by universities, governments, and enterprises. Exposed SMTP and web interfaces make compromise especially damaging because mail servers hold credentials, attachments, and password-reset links.

Recent Attack Landscape

The talk references Volexity and other reports of XSS, webshells, and authentication bypasses during mailbox imports that enabled unauthenticated remote code execution on internet-facing instances, sometimes attributed to state actors seeking data rather than financial gain.

Four Bugs in Three Months

Research across user-facing services, internal components, and inbound email processing uncovered four vulnerabilities: stored XSS via message display, authenticated SSRF chained to XSS, newline injection breaking caching to leak passwords, and archive-extractor abuse yielding RCE on any instance.

Sanitize-Send-Modify Pattern

Rather than bypassing Zimbra's Java HTML sanitizer directly, the team exploited post-sanitization transformations that reintroduced dangerous markup. Chauchefoin credits prior work by Simon Tse and promises live demos of the findings.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Thomas Chauchefoin, a vulnerability researcher at Sonar, presents a comprehensive security audit of Zimbra Collaboration Suite, an enterprise email and collaboration platform serving over 200,000 corporate, ISP, and government organizations. Chauchefoin examines the multi-tiered architecture of Zimbra, detailing attack surfaces across client-facing webmail interfaces, internal routing proxies, and message processing pipelines. The presentation documents the discovery and weaponization of four vulnerabilities: stored cross-site scripting via the "sanitize then modify" anti-pattern, post-authentication server-side request forgery (SSRF), Memcached protocol injection in custom Nginx proxies, and remote code execution via directory traversal in archive extraction.

Key Topics:
- Zimbra architecture and attack surfaces across webmail frontends, proxies, and SMTP pipelines
- Stored cross-site scripting (XSS) via the "sanitize then modify" transformation flaw
- Post-authentication Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) chained through ProxyServlet and open redirects
- Unauthenticated Memcached injection in Zimbra's custom Nginx proxy enabling cleartext credential harvesting

Technical Details:
Zimbra's webmail frontend sanitizes incoming email bodies using a server-side Java HTML sanitizer to strip dangerous elements. However, Chauchefoin identifies a critical flaw known as the "sanitize then modify" anti-pattern in the frontend's truncateBodyContent routine. After server-side sanitization, the frontend normalizes HTML inside a temporary DOM element, converts it back into a string, and executes regular expressions designed to rewrite unsecured form tags lacking action attributes. Because regex parsing operates blindly on structured text, it introduced mismatched quotes when processing crafted form tags embedded inside safe attributes. This quote imbalance broke out of the attribute context, evaluating arbitrary JavaScript whenever a victim opened an email, allowing attackers to exfiltrate mailboxes, harvest address books, and propagate worms automatically.

Chauchefoin then analyzed Zimbra's ProxyServlet, an administrative endpoint configured to proxy requests to whitelisted integration services like WebEx. While direct host manipulation was restricted, the servlet honored an X-Host HTTP header that overrode the outbound Host header. By pointing this request at a WebEx subdomain (blog.webex.com) that reflected HTTP Host headers in an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect, the internal HTTP client followed the redirect, yielding an SSRF primitive capable of querying internal cloud metadata services and backend APIs.

Turning to infrastructure, Chauchefoin uncovered a severe unauthenticated protocol injection in Zimbra's custom Nginx reverse proxy. Nginx terminates incoming HTTP, IMAP, and POP3 traffic, querying a lookup service to map users to backend mailbox servers and caching routing results in Memcached using keys formatted as route:proto:user. In certain unauthenticated endpoints, user input was passed directly into Memcached commands without newline filtering. By injecting CRLF characters (
), attackers executed arbitrary Memcached commands, including stats and set. While HTTP route destinations were strictly validated against known backends, IMAP and POP3 routes lacked validation. Attackers injected poison cache keys mapping victim accounts to attacker-controlled external IP addresses on port 1337. When desktop email clients (such as Thunderbird) connected over TLS, they transmitted cleartext usernames and passwords directly to the rogue server. Furthermore, because Nginx worker processes multiplexed requests over a single shared Memcached TCP connection, attackers used bulk get requests and cache desynchronization to poison response queues across the entire instance without prior knowledge of target usernames.

Key Takeaways:
Applications handling structured markup must never apply string-based transformations or regular expressions after sanitization has occurred, as post-processing routinely negates security sanitizers. Reverse proxies handling multi-protocol mail traffic must validate backend destinations across all supported protocols—including legacy IMAP and POP3—rather than restricting validations solely to HTTP traffic. Additionally, distributed text protocols like Memcached must enforce strict newline sanitization on cache keys and isolate connection pools between worker threads to prevent cache poisoning and state-machine desynchronization.

talks.title: 2022 - Hara-Kirin: Dissecting Huawei Mobile Devices by Maxime Peterlin & Alexandre Adamski
talks.teaser: Dissects the privileged boot chain, security hypervisor and TrustZone components of Huawei Android phones.
talks.summary:
Why Huawei devices matter

Maxime Peterlin and Alexandre Adamski of Impalabs walk through privileged components on Huawei mobile devices, motivated by the vendor's large market share and limited public research on high-end Kirin platforms. They cover boot chain, a security hypervisor, and TrustZone implementation.

Boot chain exploitation

Starting with a P30 Lite (Kirin 710), they recovered an signed but unencrypted X-loader from firmware updates. An X-modem USB recovery flaw allowed unverified payload addresses, yielding arbitrary write and code execution because boot-CPU memory was RWX. Emergency download mode via a test-point short enabled the attack path.

Hypervisor enforcement

Huawei's hypervisor keeps a read-only copy of task credentials to detect privilege escalation on syscalls or file access, restricts executable pages to kernel and module code at EL1, and hides critical peripheral memory from EL0/EL1. It enforces policy through a second stage of address translation beyond the kernel's virtual-to-intermediate mapping.

talks.title: 2022 - Attacking Safari in 2022 by Quentin Meffre
talks.teaser: Explains how Safari's layered mitigations, from JIT write protection to the JIT cage, raise the cost of browser exploitation.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how much harder it has become to gain code execution inside Safari's web content process on iPhone in 2022. It frames a browser exploit as a chain: a primitive that leaks object addresses and forges objects, an arbitrary read and write step, and then bypasses for mitigations before arbitrary code runs. The focus is the first stage, reaching code execution in the web content process.

The core of the talk is a timeline of the mitigations Safari gained from 2016 onward and how each was attacked. Early JIT write protection fell to code-reuse chaining without control flow integrity, and the hardware-enforced APR switch was bypassed by jumping into the function that set its register until shared read-only pages closed that route. The Gigacage separated typed-array buffers, but attackers moved to other object types for arbitrary writes. Structure ID randomization, pointer authentication, JIT code signing and the newer JIT cage each closed specific techniques, and the speaker notes that several bypasses were found and then fixed in hardware and software.

The closing message is that a 2022 Safari exploit needs a browser bug plus a fresh write primitive and bypasses for PAC, APR and the JIT cage, which may make a JavaScript-only next stage attractive. The speaker suggests attackers may eventually need an entry point other than the browser, though the JavaScript engine remains strong against these defenses.

talks.title: 2022 - Discovering a 0-Day in MS-RPC service by Ophir Harpaz & Stiv Kupchik
talks.teaser: Shows how a cached security callback in a Windows RPC service let a remote client reach operations meant only for local callers.
talks.summary:
The speakers examine Microsoft RPC, the decades-old remote procedure call system that Windows services use for local and network communication. They walk through interfaces, endpoints, transports and bindings, then the security model: connections are unauthenticated by default, and a server may register a security callback that checks each connection. The runtime caches that callback's result per interface, so an allowed call can let later calls skip the check.

To find candidates at scale, they built a scraper that scans binaries for RPC interface structures and reads registration flags and callback pointers, flagging servers with cached callbacks. The workstation service stood out because its callback restricts several operations to local callers. Since the service shares a host with services that register for authentication, a remote client could authenticate through a shared provider, have an allowed call cached, and then reach the restricted operations. A client flag that places the resulting network mapping in the global namespace made the effect visible. A demo showed a drive mapping created on a target that pointed to an attacker-controlled SMB server, capturing the victim's authentication.

The issue was classed as an elevation of privilege and has been patched. The team reports a few more bugs found with the same method, and over a hundred RPC servers with cached callbacks still left to examine. Future work includes automated callback analysis and fuzzing. For practitioners, the lesson is that older RPC interfaces can hide access-control gaps, and cached authorization decisions deserve scrutiny.

talks.title: 2022 - 0-click RCE on the Tesla Model 3 by David Berard & Vincent Dehors
talks.teaser: Shows a zero-click remote code execution chain against a Tesla Model 3 infotainment unit, from Wi-Fi to CAN bus commands.
talks.summary:
The talk covers a zero-click remote code execution chain against the infotainment unit of a Tesla Model 3, researched for the Pwn2Own contest. The researchers bought a unit on eBay, dumped its eMMC storage by forcing a boot from the SPI flash, and studied its Linux system and the ConnMan network manager. They focused on the Wi-Fi connectivity check, where a crafted HTTP reply could write a null byte past the end of a heap buffer.

Turning that weak primitive into code execution required heap shaping, using resized buffers and a double HTTP request trick to control neighbouring allocations. An information leak came from a DHCP hostname that ConnMan kept in memory, exposing a libc pointer and enabling further writes. A later Tesla update broke the earlier hooks, so the team switched to hijacking a timer callback to pivot the stack, then loaded a second-stage payload. For the sandbox, raw sockets bypassed iptables filtering, while netlink kernel bugs for privilege escalation were not finished before the contest.

To demonstrate impact, the team sent CAN messages through the gateway from the compromised process, opening the trunk, running the wipers and flashing the lights on a real car. ConnMan was patched weeks earlier and kernel advisories followed. The team did not win the car, as the rules did not favour their bug over an earlier entry with the same impact. The takeaway is how long a single heap bug can take to exploit and how vendor updates can break work in progress.

talks.title: 2022 - Fuzzing RDPEGFX with WTF by Colas Le Guernic & Jérémy Rubert
talks.teaser: Snapshot fuzzing on RDPEGFX explains WTF harness work, coverage trials, and a bounds overflow confirmed via MSRC.
talks.summary:
The presenters describe fuzzing Microsoft’s RDPEGFX graphics extension inside the RDP client with snapshot fuzzing in WTF, extending prior WinAFL work that struggled with unknown protocol states and unstable servers. They summarize how RDPEGFX surfaces and PDUs are structured, how WTF snapshots memory and CPU for stateful fuzzing, and their change to WTF so breakpoints work when page table entries are invalid.

Campaigns hook the GFX client decoder just before the per-PDU dispatch loop, build dumps from live sessions, and refine the harness so bad command IDs and length checks no longer abort parsing. They run repeated 24-hour experiments with naive versus improved harnesses, edge and context-sensitive coverage, and dirty-page signals, and argue crash yield matters more than basic-block curves alone.

After filtering noisy crashes, minimization isolates CreateSurface plus SolidFill PDUs that overflow a filled rectangle. Traces show the fault in the Windows software rasterizer used without 3D acceleration—an integer overflow on coordinate bounds—not in RDPEGFX parsing. They reproduce on a real client, report through MSRC, receive a bounty after validation, and offer a malicious FreeRDP proof-of-concept server without a full exploit.

talks.title: 2022 - A journey of fuzzing Nvidia graphic driver leading to LPE exploitation by Thierry Doré
talks.teaser: Shows how snapshot fuzzing of an Nvidia Windows kernel driver uncovered bugs that chain into a local privilege escalation.
talks.summary:
Thierry Doré explains why he targeted the Nvidia Windows graphics driver for fuzzing. Its entry points are simple enough to analyse without deep reversing, the attack surface is large but clearly bounded, and earlier research had already documented part of its communication protocol and found bugs. He used the WTF snapshot fuzzer, which runs code under coverage inside a virtual machine and restores memory between iterations. He chose its Bochs CPU backend because the tool is written in C++.

The kernel and user-mode components of the driver talk through the DxgkDDI escape interface, using messages with a magic tag, a size, a module tag and a command ID, with no public format. A corpus of recorded messages reached only about 40 percent coverage. To improve it, he used the Triton symbolic execution engine to invert branches in validation callbacks and generate valid messages, raising coverage to roughly 80 percent. The campaign turned up several bugs, including an out-of-bounds read that leaks data-section contents such as a stack cookie and driver pointers, and an out-of-bounds write through an unchecked array index.

He chained these bugs into a local privilege escalation. The leak let him recover the addresses he needed, and a reconstructed object redirected a function pointer, since the driver was built without control-flow guard. The final stage ran code from an executable buffer. A live demo on an RTX card under up-to-date Windows launched an elevated command prompt. Limitations included a process-ID check that forced a fresh process for each attempt. The takeaway is that snapshot fuzzing with a good input generator is within reach for non-specialists, and Nvidia fixed the reported bugs quickly.

talks.title: 2022 - Emulate it until you make it! Pwning a DrayTek Router by Philippe Laulheret
talks.teaser: Shows how a DrayTek router's firmware is unpacked and emulated to find a pre-auth remote code execution bug.
talks.summary:
The talk covers research into DrayTek routers, beginning with firmware downloaded from the vendor's website so that no device had to be opened. The speaker shows how an older image was loaded into IDA by guessing its architecture and load address, then how its decompression routine could be run inside the Unicorn emulator to recover the data. Newer images were encrypted, so a key was pulled from an early boot component and used to decrypt them. The result was a Linux system that ran QEMU to host the main bare-metal firmware.

With that environment running, the speaker focused on the web management interface and its login CGI. Credentials are base64-decoded into a stack buffer, and the expected decoded size is calculated by subtracting padding characters, so a long run of extra equals signs causes an overflow. There is no ASLR on this system, so fixed addresses could be used. The exploit sent commands to the host through a debug channel to gain a root shell, and a similar shell was reached on a purchased unit using a hidden console shortcut. The flaw appeared in firmware from mid or late 2018 and affected around 20 models, with about 200,000 devices reachable online.

Post-exploitation risks included stolen settings, DNS tampering, traffic interception and pivoting into the internal network. The vendor patched within about 30 days of notification. The practical advice is to update affected routers, avoid exposing management interfaces to the internet, and watch for login requests with abnormal base64 padding.

talks.title: 2022 - Hunting for cloudy SSRFs by Nicolas Joly
talks.teaser: Shows how SSRF flaws in Azure Kubernetes Service were hunted by tracing node-to-control-plane traffic.
talks.summary:
Nicolas Joly argues that server-side request forgery (SSRF) is a practical target when cloud services are written in memory-safe languages such as .NET, Go and Rust. He focuses on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), which splits into a Microsoft-hosted control plane and customer nodes, and says the control plane was the scope of the review.

He starts with an earlier outside case against the control plane, then describes his own failed attempt to replay API server traffic through Burp. The missing requests led him to the kubelet's outbound connections, which he inspected on Windows nodes by setting WinDbg breakpoints on socket calls and dumping plaintext from the HTTPS traffic. Health and readiness probes sent from the control plane to the nodes showed SSRF; intercepting their responses let him redirect them. He reports similar issues in kube-proxy on Linux, where he could replace the process with his own web server, and in the metrics server extension, where patching a deployment exposed many control plane pods. Microsoft fixed the probe issue in about 50 locations.

He also covers an Office Online WOPI case reported by external finders, where DNS callbacks suggested a filter. Using DNS rebinding with a zero TTL to get past an IP allowlist, and an open redirect on an Office domain, he says he reached remote code execution. He closes by urging researchers to dig into cloud components and logs, since SSRF bugs can be devastating.
